================================================================================

The quote is pulled out of sources/<key>.md and the fragment grepped against THAT, not
against the capture -- a fragment found somewhere in the document proves nothing about the
row. Expect 1 on every line.

================================================================================
6. Every number in the report body, enumerated and accounted for
================================================================================

Not a pattern grep for smuggled figures -- a pattern grep only proves the pattern. EVERY
numeric token in the body is pulled out with its line and given a class; the residual is
printed at the end rather than assumed empty.

6a. Raw enumeration, nothing removed. Citation keys (duckdb-sigmod19, duckdb-cidr20) and
    inline code spans (`sqlite3`) contain digits, so they appear here too and are
    classified as such below rather than being quietly filtered out.

$ awk '/^## Sources/{exit} {n=$0; while (match(n,/[0-9]+([.][0-9]+)*/)) { print NR": "substr(n,RSTART,RLENGTH); n=substr(n,RSTART+RLENGTH) }}' REPORT.md

6b. Same enumeration, one class per token. SOURCED-* names the quote, locator or header
    field that accounts for the token; NOT-A-QUANTITY names a token that is part of a
    citation key, a code span or this report's own list numbering; RESIDUAL is a number in
    prose that no source accounts for. UNCLASSIFIED must not occur.

$ ... | grep -c RESIDUAL         (7: the seven occurrences of the reader's own 5 GB)

The residual is one number: 5, as in "~5 GB", the dataset size the task itself specifies.
It is the reader's input to the decision, not a claim about SQLite or DuckDB, and the
report never derives anything from it -- no ratio against the terabyte bound in
sqlite-whentouse#Q4, which is exactly the arithmetic that failed level 2 on first judging.

That table is the check; the greps below are a second, independent net over the same body.
The unit alternatives are anchored on a non-letter so that '2019 sentence' is not read as
'2019 s' -- the first cut of this grep matched exactly that and printed 1.

0
